title: Sorry, Haters
full_review:
"Sorry, Haters" (InDigEnt) is several notches better than its off-putting title might suggest, but this study of post-Sept. 11 anxiety, makes for uneasy, ultimately pointless viewing.

The murky tale begins with well-educated Muslim taxi driver Ashade (Abdellatif Kechiche) picking up Phoebe (Robin Wright Penn), a distraught television executive, who asks him to drive her from New York across the river to New Jersey.

She seems uncertain where she wants to go, but she finally asks him to stop in front of a suburban home, where she sadly views a happy domestic scene. When the family goes inside, she gets out, walks purposefully toward the house and defaces the family's car with a rock.

Eventually, she calms herself and begins to open up. She tells Ashade she's a programming executive for an MTV-like network where she produces a popular show called "Sorry, Haters," showing how the rich spend their money.

She indulgently agrees to allow Ashade to drop something off at his sister-in-law Eloise's (Elodie Bouchez) apartment on the return trip. When she gets out of the car herself and asks to use Eloise's bathroom, she learns that Ashade's doctor brother has been unjustly imprisoned for contact with a terror suspect, leaving Ashade to take care of his sister-in-law.

Phoebe insists on helping him extricate the brother, and calls a high-powered lawyer she says can help.

This seemingly kind deed leads to bizarre complications Ashade could not have imagined.

Writer-director Jeff Stanzler has created a twisty film with serious intent, but what he's trying to say isn't exactly clear. Though there are several wonderfully taut scenes, including a revealing lunch Phoebe has with her business colleague, Phyllis (Sandra Oh), the movie fails to satisfy on a dramatic level.

Penn gives a well-shaded and complex performance, and there's good work by Kechiche and Oh. It's admirable that Arab stereotypes have been avoided, and the Ashade character is so sympathetic, which was one of Stanzler's stated goals in making the film, though the good-looking Kechiche's accent makes comprehension a little difficult at times.

"Haters" takes some time getting started, and the sheer unpleasantness of the story will turn off many viewers. Sorry.

The film has rough and crude language, alcohol use, ethnic slurs, violence and sexual situations. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
